brief.head: Not like the movies
brief.text: Popular culture and films “completely get it wrong”, Amit Varma said. Poker tests the mind with game theory and mathematics, and is also “a great test of character”. {038-J08}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on poker’s lessons for life
lead.head: Play the hand, not the outcome
body: Ajay Shah opened with flattery. Listeners wanted an episode on poker, he said, “because one of us is a genius and knows a hell of a lot about poker.” {038-J01}

Amit Varma objected. The golden rule, he said, is to underpromise and overdeliver. He was no genius, but he had played poker seriously for many years and loved the game, while having conflicting thoughts about it.

What followed was a stripped-down presentation on the foundations of poker, and then a conversation about what they teach. Poker, Shah said, is a small game hiding a metaphor about life, “because life actually is a play of probability.”
## The arithmetic of a hand
The first big lesson, Varma said, is expected value. Toss a fair coin: heads, he pays you 51 paise; tails, you pay him 49. Over 100 flips you would be up a paisa a flip, so the bet is “plus EV”.
Lose the toss and you have still chosen well. “You made the right decision and you got unlucky,” Varma said. {038-C01}
The same sum decides whether to call a bet with a flush draw, and explains why aggression pays: a raise that makes a better hand fold wins the pot too.

Then came game theory. A player whose range holds bluffs and value hands in exactly the right proportions cannot lose in the long run, whatever his opponent holds. It is almost impossible for a human to play that way, so real poker is a contest of spotting and exploiting each other’s deviations.
## A game of the mind
Maths is not the whole of it. “In theory, poker is all about the numbers. In practice, though, it’s a mental game,” Varma said. {038-C05}
The enemy is tilt, the anger that turns good players into bad ones. Loss aversion feeds it, because a loss hurts more than an equal win pleases.

He ended with a caution. When he started playing, he said, only about 5 per cent of players were long-term winners. By the time he left, he saw that many winners leave, while the losers stay, because they are addicted.
## Three lessons for life
In the conversation that followed, Varma drew three lessons from the table. The first is to acknowledge the role of luck, and then to focus only on what you can control.
The second is to think probabilistically. Hindsight makes the past look inevitable, but before a die lands, every number has its chance. {038-C08}
The third is to put in volume. A hand between the world’s best player and a beginner is roughly 51-49, so the edge shows only over a large sample. {#novice}

Shah had already arrived at the same place through finance. Many small bets, each right 51 per cent of the time, beat one big bet held with full conviction, as long as they are not all drawn from one correlated idea.

Then Varma named the tragedy. In poker he could play a million hands. Life often does not allow such a sample, and mostly everything is luck: the skill lies in how well one plays the cards one is dealt.
Where volume is impossible, Shah said, be zen. “Don’t beat yourself up and don’t go raging against life and the world. It just is.”
Varma, thinking aloud, wondered how somebody beats themselves up. Then he signed off: “next time.”

second.label: Poker and finance
second.head: The 51 per cent solution
second.deck: Ajay Shah’s case for many small bets over one big conviction
body: Ajay Shah carried Amit Varma’s poker lessons into finance, citing what he believed was Mark Twain’s line: if you must forecast, forecast often. {038-J04}

The usual mistake, Shah said, is to stay cautious and commit only when absolutely sure, which he called a delusion. Efficient markets theory teaches that pricing mistakes are small, so even 51 per cent is hard to reach. Better, then, to hold many small positions with a 51 per cent chance each than one giant position held with full conviction. {038-C11}

But the law of large numbers needs independent draws. Shuffling guarantees that in poker. In finance, one mindset can make a hundred bets flow from one correlated idea, leaving only an illusion of diversification. {038-C12}

quote.text: So what you can control is the number of ideas. And the extent to which they’re correlated.

second.caption: many small bets

third.head: All bets are on
body: When people dismiss poker as gambling, Amit Varma has two answers. First, it is a game of skill. Second, what is wrong with gambling? {038-C09}

If gambling means acting on probabilistic judgements, Varma said, we all do it every day. Crossing the road carries a chance of being hit by a truck, greater than the risk of an air accident, and yet we cross. {#truck}
Approach a pretty girl at a bar, and you are weighing a range of possible responses. “You buy a house, it’s a gamble. You make a friend, it’s a gamble,” he said. {#house}

Every action, with its opportunity costs piled up, is a gamble. Most of us think probabilistically without admitting it, he argued, and admitting it would help us stop blaming ourselves for past decisions that went wrong.
third.caption: everyday gambles

sections.label: Expected value
sections.head: The coin that pays a paisa
sections.caption: expected value and equity
body: The first big lesson of poker, Amit Varma said, is probabilistic thinking, and it begins with expected value. Offer a fair coin: heads, you win 51 paise; tails, you pay 49. Over 100 flips you expect to be up 100 paise, a paisa a flip, so the bet is plus-EV. {038-C01}
If it lands tails, you were unlucky, not wrong. Keep making plus-EV decisions and you win in the long run.
At the table, say you hold ace-ten of hearts with two hearts on the flop. Nine hearts remain unseen, and one of them arrives by the river about 38 per cent of the time. {#hearts}

An opponent shoves 10,000 into a 10,000 pot. You must call 10,000 to win 20,000, so you need to be right a third of the time: an easy call. Had he bet 20,000, you would need 40 per cent, and it would be just about a fold.
## Make him fold

Your chance of winning applied to the pot is your pot equity. Fold equity is what you win when your raise makes the other player give up, and it can turn a losing all-in into a profitable one. {038-C02}
So there are two reasons to bet: for value, to make a worse hand call, or as a bluff, to make a better hand fold.
~ Position adds information. The player on the dealer button acts last, and the later you act, Varma said, the weaker the hands you can play. {038-C03}

quote.text: You don’t have to make the best hand to win. Making the other guy fold also works.

sections.label: Game theory
sections.head: Bluff by the numbers
sections.caption: game theory and bluffing
body: Watch popular cinema and you might think poker is all about spotting tells and bluffs, Amit Varma said. Apply game theory, and you need not even think about your opponent’s cards. {#cinema}

Suppose he bets 100 into a pot of 200 on the river. His opponent gets three to one on a call and must be right 25 per cent of the time to break even. If Varma’s range is exactly 25 per cent bluffs and 75 per cent value hands, he cannot lose, whatever the other player does. {#range}
For a pot-sized bet the right mix is one-third bluffs. A balanced range, he said, is not a mix of good and bad hands; it is one with the proportions right.
In rock, paper, scissors, the optimal strategy is to be totally random. In football, penalty-takers randomise, so goalkeepers must too. {#rps}
## Exploit, and be exploited

It is almost impossible for a human to play this game theory optimal, or GTO, poker, so real poker is exploitative. If an opponent folded too much, Varma would bluff him more; if he called too much, Varma would bet more for value.

~ Every deviation can be punished, his own included. {038-C04} A rival who noticed him bluffing more could start calling more. That, he said, is much of the fun: mental games of figuring each other out.

quote.text: But equally when I am exploitative, I am also exploitable because I am also deviating from GTO.

sections.label: The mental game
sections.head: When the maths isn’t enough
sections.caption: tilt and the mental game
body: Human beings play poker, Amit Varma said, and human beings are frail and flawed. Their weakness at the table has a name: tilt, a loss of composure, usually from anger, that leads to bad decisions and lost money. {038-C05}

Poker puts an unusual load on the emotions. In most fields a bad day on March 15 is no big deal; in poker it can cost you everything you earned in January and February, especially since most players he knows do not manage their bankroll. {#bankroll}
That can feel devastating to men whose ego is tied to money as status and to winning. Loss aversion makes it worse.
## The entitled player
Varma’s own weakness was entitlement tilt: sitting down armed with maths and game theory, only to fume at bad beats from players who knew none of it. {038-S02}

His closing caution was about addiction. When he started, he said, only about 5 per cent of players were long-term winners; by the time he left, he saw that many of them moved on, while the losers stayed. {038-S03}
~ He also urged viewers to check the law. When he last checked, live poker in India was possible only in the offshore casinos of Goa and in Sikkim. {#goa}

quote.text: Mastering the math is not enough. You also have to master the mind.

sections.label: The first lesson
sections.head: Neither fate nor fault
sections.caption: acknowledging luck
body: Ajay Shah pushed Amit Varma one level beyond the game. Poker is a small game, he said, but inside it hides a metaphor about life. Varma replied with three lessons.
The first is to acknowledge luck. Poker is a game of skill, Varma said, but the quantum of luck is so high that the skill lies in managing it. Life is no different. {038-C06}
Misread luck and you pay either way. Good fortune makes us arrogant and complacent. Bad fortune makes us defeatist, or gives us imposter syndrome.
## Dharma, not destiny

The answer is not fatalism. Poker players are taught not to be results-oriented, and Varma reached for a pairing: “Lord Krishna and Spike Lee would be in agreement over this.” Do the right thing, and don’t worry about the fruits of your action. {038-J03}
Your dharma, he said, is to do your best and be equanimous about the rest, almost in a Buddhist way. Much unhappiness comes from not accepting consequences we do not control.
~ Nor is bad luck a sign of fate, he said. In his column *Unlikely is Inevitable*, he described the law of truly large numbers: with enough iterations, the most unlikely things will happen. {038-R04}

quote.text: I would go as far as to say that ninety-eight or ninety-nine percent of everything that happens to us is sheer luck.

sections.label: The second lesson
sections.head: The die is still in the air
sections.caption: thinking in probabilities
body: Amit Varma’s second lesson is to think probabilistically. Hindsight bias makes everything in the past look inevitable, because once something is over it has either happened or it hasn’t. {038-C08}
Before that, there were only probabilities. A die that lands on five has 100 per cent landed on five, but while it is in the air every number has an even chance.
Nor does the charge that poker is gambling trouble him. “What’s wrong with gambling? We are all gambling,” he said. {038-C09} Every action, with its opportunity costs, is a gamble.
Admitting this, Varma argued, stops us blaming ourselves for past decisions that went wrong, and putting numbers on important decisions brings clarity about what we are doing and why. {#clarity}
## Shah’s markets
Ajay Shah had pre-empted the point, Varma said, by taking it into markets. Many small bets, each right 51 per cent of the time, work out better than one big bet held with full conviction. {038-C11}

~ The catch is independence. Shuffling guarantees it in poker; in finance, a hundred bets can all flow from one correlated idea. What remains, Shah said, “is up to Lady Luck, and then you just should be zen about it.” {038-C12}

quote.text: After something has happened, it has 100% happened or it has zero percent happened, which means it’s not happened.

sections.label: The third lesson
sections.head: A million hands, one life
sections.caption: putting in volume
body: The third lesson is to put in volume. Amit Varma would lose a hundred points of tennis to Nadal, and a hundred games of chess to Magnus Carlsen, “even though I’m a good recreational player”. {038-J05}
Poker is different. A hand between the best player in the world and someone who just learned the rules is about 51-49. {#novice} The edge shows only over a large sample.
So every decision should aim to be plus-EV, he said, and a player must stay deeply self-critical, because an assumption, a premise or the maths may be wrong.
## Doors for creators

For creators, volume pays twice. Constant iteration makes you better, and each new video or blog post is another chance of going viral. This does not mean spreading yourself everywhere, which Varma called daft, but putting volume into what you are passionate about. {038-C13}

Then the tragedy. In poker he could play a million hands, and at one point he played several tables at once online. Life rarely allows such a sample. He and Shah, he said, were dealt incredibly good starting hands, and their dharma is to make the most of them and help others. {038-C14}
~ Where high numbers are not a choice, Shah said, be a little zen: don’t beat yourself up, and accept those lotteries.

quote.text: If you have many doors, opportunity will knock somewhere or the other.

side.boxText: Amit Varma promised no fancy animation and no funky graphics. His presentation runs from the basic rules of No Limit Hold’em through terminology, probabilistic thinking, game theory and the mental game, to a note of caution. {#stripped}

contQuote.text: The tragic lesson of poker is that mostly everything is luck, and your skill only applies to how well you play the cards that you’re dealt.

stories.caption: the delusion machine
stories.kicker: Amit Varma answers a question Ajay Shah once asked him
stories.head: The delusion machine
body: Ajay Shah once asked Amit Varma a question. Why do bad players bet money on poker, but never on chess? {038-S01}

In chess, Varma answered, you get immediate feedback with every game about how good you are. The Elo ratings on the major chess sites and in competitive chess are pretty accurate, so every player knows his level, and a bad player won’t be stupid enough to bet against a better one.

Poker is also a game of skill, but luck plays a much bigger part. In poker terms, the variance is high, and skill shows only in the long run. Every bad player has lucky hands, lucky sessions, even lucky months, and many end up believing they are good when they are not.
~ Good players guard against this, Varma said. They train themselves to think in terms of expected value, and keep making good decisions without worrying about short-term outcomes. {#train}
stories.why: Noise hides ability. Where luck is loud and feedback is slow, people mistake good fortune for skill. Applied to life, Varma said, thinking in probabilities helps us decide better and makes us equanimous about outcomes. {038-C07}
stories.postscript: So strong is that detachment, he suggested, that understanding poker could be “the route to Buddhism”.

stories.caption: entitlement tilt
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the kind of tilt that undid his maths
stories.head: Undone by a Diwali amateur
body: Amit Varma knows tilt from the inside. Of its many kinds, the one he was personally prone to is called entitlement tilt. {038-S02}
He would go into a game armed with all his maths, his game theory and his knowledge of ranges. Across the table might sit a player who knew none of it, treating poker as a festive card game.
In Varma’s words: “some idiot who knows none of this and is playing it like Teen Patti on Diwali would give me five bad beats in a hand and I played correctly.” {038-J02}
Then, he said, he would be fuming, and would actually start playing badly and losing money.
~ There are many kinds of tilt, he added, and a player needs to know what they all are and watch out for them in himself. All the cognitive biases come into play too.
stories.why: Knowing the correct play does not protect you from how you react to a bad outcome. Believing you deserve to win because you did things right is a trap of its own: the mind needs mastering too. {038-C05}

stories.end: you have an addictive personality, be careful, don't play this game.
stories.caption: why winners leave the game
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on what five years at the tables taught him
stories.head: The winners cash out
body: Amit Varma played poker seriously between 2010 and 2015, and even wrote a regular column on it for the *Economic Times*. {#years}

When he started, he fell in love with the mathematical side of the game. Looking at the ecosystem, he saw that only about 5 per cent of players were long-term winners. He assumed that over a long period those winners would stay in the game and the losers would rotate out. {038-S03}

By the time he left, years later, he had realised the opposite was true. Many winners move on, because the qualities that make them good at poker serve them elsewhere. The losers stay, because they are addicted.
Gambling addiction, he said, is “a terrible, terrible thing”, and he has seen lives destroyed by it.
~ His advice was plain: if you think you have an addictive personality, be careful, and don’t play this game.

quote.text: Many winning players leave because what makes them good at poker also makes them good at other things, so they move on.

stories.postscript: His final column for the *Economic Times*, *Why I Loved and Left Poker*, may, he said, tell you why you shouldn’t start playing. {038-R02}

quiz.q: Heads you win 51 paise, tails you pay 49. What is the bet’s expected value per flip?
quiz.a: One paisa a flip: a plus-EV bet, worth taking even if you lose.

quiz.q: Why, according to Amit Varma, do bad players bet on poker but never on chess?
quiz.a: Chess ratings tell everyone their level; poker’s high variance lets bad players think they’re good.

quiz.q: What are the two kinds of equity Varma described in his presentation?
quiz.a: Pot equity, your chance of winning applied to the pot, and fold equity.

quiz.q: What kind of tilt was Amit Varma personally prone to at the poker table?
quiz.a: Entitlement tilt: fuming at bad beats from players who knew none of the maths.

quiz.q: Which three lessons for life did Varma draw from his years of playing poker?
quiz.a: Acknowledge the role of luck, think probabilistically, and put in volume.

quiz.q: What hidden condition must hold, Ajay Shah warned, for many small bets to work?
quiz.a: The bets must be independent; correlated ideas only create an illusion of diversification.
